title: Road Rage: GRRRR!!!
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss road rage and aggressive driving, drawing on a HowStuffWorks article by Jonathan Strickland. They cover the term's recent origin and the 1990s "epidemic" talk, psychologist Leon James ("Doctor Driving") and his views on how culture and parents model aggressive driving, catharsis theory, fight-or-flight and anger as a seductive emotion, and situational triggers like immobility, lack of control, territoriality, and ambiguity of apologies. They walk through escalation from impatience to power struggles to violence, the effect of guns on aggressive driving, and tips for avoiding road rage (calm music, leaving early, not making eye contact, being the bigger person). They close with horn design, safety seats, Auto Vantage courtesy rankings, statistics by gender, and listener mail about the Wow! signal.

segments.title: Hosts' driver types and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, joke about three kinds of drivers (good, bad or nervous, and jerks), and discuss how a driver can be provoked and the danger of running afoul of a violent driver, citing a cell phone video of a shooting.

segments.title: Origins of the term and the road rage epidemic
segments.summary: The term road rage is recent, traced to the early 1990s, and became nationally known in the nineties amid talk of an epidemic. The hosts note that road rage is specific to driving and cannot simply be extrapolated to other settings.

segments.title: Car psychology, Doctor Driving and cultural causes
segments.summary: Leon James, known as Doctor Driving and an expert witness to Congress on traffic psychology, argues that culture's view of aggressive driving is a major cause. Children see parents change behavior behind the wheel, and movies and TV normalize aggressive driving. The barrier of the car gives a sense of anonymity and confidence.

segments.title: Catharsis theory, fight or flight, and anger
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Freud's idea of venting emotion, which research suggests is wrong; venting may train aggression. They describe how fight-or-flight responses, a sense of territory, and the seductive adrenaline of anger drive road rage, and note that it is a real but context-specific phenomenon.

segments.title: Escalation and the road rage killer
segments.summary: Road rage typically involves a trigger and an escalating series of aggressive actions. The hosts describe the so-called road rage killer, who chased Timothy Davison for about fifteen miles through Maryland and Pennsylvania before shooting him.

segments.title: Causes: immobility, constriction, lack of control, territoriality
segments.summary: Dr. James identifies driving factors that contribute to road rage: immobility, feeling boxed in, lack of control over traffic and other drivers, and the inability to abandon the car. Territoriality, denial and loss of objectivity, and unpredictability are also discussed.

segments.title: Apologies, merging, blocking the box and tailgating
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the ambiguity of apology gestures and waves, letting drivers merge, not blocking intersections, and the lack of a legal or quantified definition of tailgating, including Georgia's two-car-length rule taught in driver's ed.

segments.title: Defining road rage and Dr. James's three levels
segments.summary: Strickland's definition ties road rage to aggressive driving that leads to violence. The hosts offer their own broader definitions. Dr. James's three levels are impatience and inattentiveness, power struggles such as eye contact and gestures, and recklessness that escalates into violence. A study finds guns in cars increase aggressive driving, and Professor Emil Cakaro advises not assuming the other driver is rational.

segments.title: Preventing road rage and car horns
segments.summary: Tips include avoiding eye contact, controlling temper, being the bigger person, leaving early, playing relaxing music, and not venting. The hosts discuss improved car horn designs, including a Tesla pedestrian horn, a friendlier chirp, and an apology signal light idea.

segments.title: Listener mail on the Wow! signal and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener mail from radio astronomer Emily Petrov discusses the Wow! signal, noting the Big Ear telescope detected it in one of two sky positions and that microwave ovens have caused radio interference. The hosts close with contact details.
